newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan bankers see higher interest rates.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan bankers see higher interest rates.

text.p: Pakistan may have to raise yields on securities traded in the interbank market to attract foreign currency deposits from abroad after the IMF halted payments on its standby loan, bankers said on Saturday.
"The government will have to raise the rupee cut-off rates to maintain the spreads banks get by bringing in swap deposits," forex analyst Umer Ehtesham of Banque Indosuez told Reuters.
An International Monetary Fund mission left Islamabad on Friday without making a public statement after two weeks of talks to review Pakistan's economic performance.
Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz said the standby loan had been effectively suspended and the next few months would see a transition to a longer-term structural adjustment loan.
Ehtesham said the absence of IMF funds meant Pakistan would have to rely on foreign currency brought in by banks from abroad as the main source of its foreign currency requirements.
Banks swap these foreign currency inflows for rupees, which are then used to lend to the corporate sector or to buy government securities in the interbank money market.
Six-month short-term federal bonds were last auctioned at a weighted average yield of 16.45 percent a year compared to a yield of 16.50 percent in the previous auction.
"Breaking with the IMF would mean a substantial increase in the risk portfolio of Pakistan," Ehtesham said, adding that banks would find it harder to source foreign currency for Pakistan.
"For a higher risk, a higher return is expected." he added.
A foreign banker, who asked not to be identified, said international lenders would now be seeking returns above 200 basis points over LIBOR (London interbank offered rate).
He said higher yields on six-month bonds would fuel inflation, running at 13.83 percent in February year-on-year, compared to 9.76 percent in February 1996.

Analysts said international donors could react negatively to the IMF decision, despite the fund's agreement to begin talks on a softer, medium-term lending programme after Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government has unveiled its economic strategy.
"The IMF's decision is very likely to have a bad impact on the lending plans of the World Bank and the Aid-to-Pakistan Consortium expected to meet in April," the foreign banker said.
Pakistan expected to get loans worth $2.5 billion from the World Bank for capital markets and financial sector reform and another $2.8 billion from the Aid-to-Pakistan Consortium.
Ehtesham said not many banks around the world would be keen to provide Pakistan even short-term loans at the moment.
"The last time we brought in a large amount, we went round to some 400 banks and found only a few who have any limits left for Pakistan," he said.
Bankers say Pakistan, with liquid reserves of $1.15 billion, faces debt payments of about $1.6 billion by end-June.
Aziz told Reuters on Friday Pakistan would have no short-term problem in managing its balance of payments, but long-term stability required higher growth and exports.
